claims.text: Melt spinning at cooling rates of 10^5–10^6 K/s produces an amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 structure.
The as-quenched amorphous alloy contains residual internal stresses.
The as-quenched alloy has metastable short-range atomic order.
Picosecond-scale laser pulses applied immediately after melt-spinning quenching will increase amorphous retention.
Post-quench picosecond laser pulses will increase the alloy's thermal stability.
The laser-induced transient temperature rise should remain below approximately 30 K above the amorphous stability limit.
Laser pulsing will cause transient relaxation of residual stress.
Laser pulsing will promote local atomic rearrangement into a more stable amorphous short-range order.
Picosecond pulse duration is too short to permit significant atomic diffusion.
Suppressing significant atomic diffusion will prevent nucleation of primary crystalline phases.
A post-quench laser treatment will prevent primary crystalline-phase formation during rapid cooling.
Laser treatment will reduce crystallization-exotherm intensity relative to untreated melt-spun samples.
Laser treatment will increase the DSC crystallization-onset temperature relative to untreated melt-spun samples.
Rapidly quenched Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits extensive primary crystallization without the intervention.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits a complex, multistep crystallization sequence upon reheating.
Slow cooling produces a complex crystalline microstructure containing multiple phases.
The laser intervention is restricted to samples melt-spun at 10^5–10^6 K/s.
Subsequent DSC reheating should remain within approximately 30 K above the crystallization onset or amorphous stability boundary.
Nonuniform laser-energy deposition could cause local overheating.
Scalable integration of ultrafast laser treatment with melt spinning has not been demonstrated.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field says melt spinning at 10^5–10^6 K/s produces an amorphous structure, whereas the baseline says the rapidly quenched alloy shows extensive primary crystallization. The cited records support the former description.
The intervention is applied only after melt-spinning quenching, but the mechanism claims that it prevents crystalline phases from forming during the preceding rapid-cooling step.
